newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela's S.Africa secures first World Bank loan.
newsitem.headline: Mandela's S.Africa secures first World Bank loan.

text.p: The World Bank has approved its first loan to post-apartheid South Africa -- $46 million to help boost the country's industrial competitiveness, the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) said on Friday.
The 15-year loan, which carries a three-year grace period, will be aimed primarily at small and medium businesses which have proved successful in other countries at breaking into export markets.
South African industry, protected in the apartheid era by high tariff barriers, is today fighting an uphill battle to compete in the global marketplace.
According to the World Economic Forum's 1997 World Competitivesness Report, South Africa ranked 44th among the world's top 53 competitive nations.

Two of the programmes which the loan will finance over four years aim to address the problem by providing government assistance of 50 to 65 percent towards in the cost of securing specialist marketing and technical advice.

"We find that many firms are struggling in coping with international competition and one of the reasons that they are struggling is they are not able to get the information or strategic advice that they need," said Alan Hirsch, DTI chief director of industry and technology strategy.
A third programme will provide additional short-term export guarantee finance to smaller businesses to help them gain a foothold in export markets.
Hirsch told Reuters that small- and medium-sized firms had the potential to be significant exporters but they had difficulties raising money from banks.
"We are basically making it easier for banks to lend to smaller companies. It's something we think is very important."
The loan falls within South Africa's existing borrowing limit and will help improve and diversify the government's foreign debt portfolio, officials said.

World Bank representative Judith Edstrom said the country had access to relatively high levels of concessional finance -- it is currently negotiating a 750 million rand ($168 million) loan with the African Development Bank -- but the World Bank loan made sense within the overall borrowing strategy.

"South Africa does have to borrow on foreign markets as part of its debt strategy and I think it's recognised that the (World) Bank's terms are competitive and part of the borrowing should be from the international finance institutions," she said.
Edstrom said discussions had been held on further help in the area of municipal infrastructure but Pretoria's primary interest lay in technical cooperation with the Bank.

South Africa secured 11 loans from the World Bank in the 1950s and 1960s, mainly in the power and telecommunications sector. But the programme came to a halt as international opposition to the aparthied regime built up. The last loan was repaid in 1968.
President Nelson Mandela's government, elected in 1994, now has a much wider choice in financing and has already launched several international bonds.
This year it plans to tap the Japanese yen and dollar markets to provide four billion rand in offshore finance to help cover the 1997/98 budget deficit.
